title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
abstract: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
abstract: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.

title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?
abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \ourmethod, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

title: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics
abstract: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

title: OpenNWM: A Generalist Navigation World Model with Latent Action Pretraining
abstract: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.

title: LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environments via Modular Recombination
abstract: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet existing environments are designed for specific tasks and fail to generalize to new ones. Recent methods automate environment construction with LLMs. However, they generate each environment from scratch, neither reusing parts shared across environments nor carrying a fix from one environment to the rest. To address this, we propose a new paradigm of evolving environment atoms, which composes environments from reusable atoms (intent, rule, data and server) and evolves the atoms when an environment fails to give reliable feedback (e.g., an application lacks a tool the task requires). To instantiate this paradigm, we introduce LegoEnv, which builds 5,465 verified environments over 223 applications, and one round of evolution raises the share of solvable environments from 71.6% to 88.3%. On AutomationBench, SFT on these environments lifts Qwen3.6-27B from 16.0% to 32.0%, and RL with their verifiers lifts Qwen3.8-27B from 37.6% to 40.3%. Further analyses show steady gains with corpus size, transfer to unseen applications, and failures concentrated in a few shared root causes.

title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

title: MemHarmBench: Evaluating Cross-Session Prompt Injection in Memory-Persistent AI Agents
abstract: AI agents often rely on persistent memory to retain user preferences and operational rules across sessions. However, this capability introduces a new safety risk: malicious instructions from messages, documents, or Web content can be retained in memory and influence future tasks even after the original attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics, however, fail to capture who is affected and how attacks translate into downstream harm during otherwise normal task execution. We introduce MemHarmBench, a victim-centric benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. MemHarmBench considers three categories of potential victims: users, workspace/project owners, and external stakeholders. Our evaluation first exposes an agent to malicious instructions and tests whether they are retained in memory. We then remove the attack content and initiate a new session with a legitimate task while preserving the agent's memory. We jointly evaluate whether the agent follows the attacker's intent, completes the legitimate task, and exhibits observable execution anomalies. title: FinForesight: A Diagnostic Backtesting Benchmark for Deep Research Systems in Financial Forecasting
abstract: Anticipating financial outcomes requires synthesizing evolving evidence and reasoning under uncertainty, making deep research systems promising tools for forecasting. Yet evaluating forecasting ability is challenging because historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or information retrieved after the forecast date. Live forecasting avoids direct access to realized outcomes, but feedback arrives only after events resolve. To obtain timely feedback and assess historical scores, we introduce FinForesight, a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. Across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, the benchmark evaluates four forecasting tasks: valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately from forecasting performance. Our harness-compatible framework restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff, and live evaluations to test whether controlled backtests approximate future performance. Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results. Forecasting attribution and robustness analyses reveal how scores respond to retrieval policy and how predictions respond to prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. The code and benchmark data are publicly available.

title: QFabric: Guarded Cross-Domain Task Recovery and Its Limits on a Linux-RTOS Board
abstract: Heterogeneous embedded boards pair a Linux application processor with a real-time microcontroller (MCU), which suggests moving a task between the two domains when its timing degrades. We present QFabric, a prototype that treats cross-domain placement as guarded recovery from a violated empirical soft real-time contract: a bounded task is compiled for both domains, monitored in windows with hysteresis, switched only after semantic and capacity admission at a quiescent epoch boundary, and committed or rolled back after probation. On an Arduino UNO Q (Cortex-A53 Linux and a Cortex-M33 running Zephyr), we characterize the stock Bridge RPC interconnect and measure five workloads in both domains under idle, CPU-load, and higher-priority SCHED_FIFO contention, with ordinary and real-time callers. Each MCU invocation costs about 19 ms of dispatch regardless of compute, the MCU runs the heaviest kernel 34x slower, and because every call traverses Linux userspace, Linux contention inflates the MCU path far more than the Linux path (p99 up to 400 ms versus 17.0 ms). Across 30 cells of a four-node chain, Linux meets every contract within 0.8% misses and QFabric correctly never migrates; a controller without hysteresis migrates in 7 cells, raising p95 by up to 177x, and probation rolls back 5 of those moves. On Linux-dispatched heterogeneous boards, migration therefore cannot isolate a task from Linux interference, and recovery guards matter chiefly by preventing harmful moves. This paper supersedes an earlier artifact release whose reported improvement arose from measurement defects that we identify. All source, raw traces, and generators are public.

title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches 15.0times the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches 1.065C while every control stays within C, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields varepsilon lower bounds (3.25 at δ=10^{-5}) below the advertised guarantee (4.38). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.

title: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on τ^3-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.

title: Necessity–Uncertainty Theory of Information: A Conceptual Framework
abstract: Abstract: Information is often defined as the reduction of uncertainty. This paper argues that uncertainty alone does not fully explain the emergence or value of information. Necessity—the contextual demand to resolve uncertainty—must also be considered. By combining these two dimensions, we propose a simple formula: \[I = N \cdot U\] Here, \(U\) represents uncertainty measured through Shannon entropy, while \(N\) reflects the situational need for information on a scale from 0 to 1. The framework suggests that information arises, and matters, only when uncertainty exists and necessity requires resolution. Examples from communication, decision-making, and knowledge acquisition illustrate the theory’s relevance and practical scope. This framework extends Shannon’s theory by adding a human-centered dimension. It bridges mathematical information theory with epistemology and decision sciences. Everyday interactions—such as tutoring, communication, or decision-making—provide living evidence of the theory. Information is not merely an abstract reduction of entropy; it is the synthesis of uncertainty and necessity within real contexts of human inquiry. title: Deep Learning for Sequential Decision Making Under Uncertainty: Foundations, Frameworks, and Frontiers
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving increasingly beyond prediction to support decisions in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments. This shift creates a natural intersection with operations research and management sciences (OR/MS), which have long offered conceptual and methodological foundations for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. At the same time, recent advances in deep learning, including feedforward neural networks, LSTMs, transformers, and deep reinforcement learning, have expanded the scope of data-driven modeling and opened new possibilities for large-scale decision systems. This tutorial presents an OR/MS-centered perspective on deep learning for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. Its central premise is that deep learning is valuable not as a replacement for optimization, but as a complement to it. Deep learning brings adaptability and scalable approximation, whereas OR/MS provides the structural rigor needed to represent constraints, recourse, and uncertainty. The tutorial reviews key decision-making foundations, connects them to the major neural architectures in modern AI, and discusses leading approaches to integrating learning and optimization. It also highlights emerging impact in domains such as supply chains, healthcare and epidemic response, agriculture, energy, and autonomous operations. More broadly, it frames these developments as part of a wider transition from predictive AI toward decision-capable AI and highlights the role of OR/MS in shaping the next generation of integrated learning–optimization systems.

title: Accelerating noisy variational quantum algorithms with physics-informed denoising networks
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are promising for near-term quantum computing, but are severely limited by hardware noise and the substantial circuit overhead required for error mitigation methods such as Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE). We propose a Physics-Informed Denoising Network (PIDN) that reduces the cost of ZNE by learning a surrogate model of its optimization dynamics. By viewing the variational update as a trajectory in the parameter space, PIDN is trained to reproduce ZNE-mitigated expectation values and gradient directions while incorporating a physics-informed loss that preserves the gradient descent dynamics. Once trained, PIDN replaces repeated multi-noise evaluations with denoised expectation and gradient estimation directly from the current noisy observation and the historical trajectory, significantly reducing circuit executions. We benchmark the approach on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm for 3-regular graphs, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, and transverse-field Ising models, as well as the variational quantum eigensolver for LiH, BeH$_2$ and H$_2$O. Across all tasks, PIDN attains performance comparable to ZNE, while reducing the number of circuit executions by a factor of approximately 4 to 6. Gradient cosine similarity with ZNE remains above 0.95 throughout training. Robustness analysis shows that PIDN fails only when ZNE itself becomes unreliable, and ablation studies confirm the necessity of the physics-informed loss for maintaining directional consistency. We further find that PIDN tracks optimization dynamics most accurately when the effective loss landscape retains strong low-frequency structure. These results establish PIDN as a scalable, resource-efficient strategy for noise-resilient variational optimization in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum regime.

title: Unconditional authentication in quantum key distribution via hybrid entangled physical unclonable functions
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) enables Information-Theoretically Secure (ITS) key exchange, robust even against future quantum computing threats. However, a fundamental limitation of QKD is the requirement for an authenticated classical channel, which necessitates a pre-shared secret key. In this work, we address this challenge by adopting a Hybrid Entangled Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) protocol for authentication. We demonstrate that this PUF-based method generates an ITS initial key under minimal explicit hardware assumptions. This approach allows us to experimentally perform a fully ITS-authenticated entanglement-based QKD protocol that relies solely on such assumptions, effectively eliminating the need for pre-shared secrets. This represents a significant step towards the practical realization of quantum network protocols using lightweight, readily available hardware assumptions, without weakening security guarantees.

title: Multi-dimensional hierarchical temporal alignment for improved temporal commonsense reasoning in large language models
abstract: Benefiting from recent advances in generative AI and large language models (LLMs), current LLM-driven AI systems are rapidly reshaping how we reason, plan, and make decisions. Yet endowing these systems with human-like temporal intelligence (e.g., understanding and comparing events across time) remains largely unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Multi-dimensional Hierarchical Temporal Alignment framework (denoted as MHTA), of which the core idea is to effectively ground the temporal alignment of an LLM in both event-specific and cross-event real-world temporal commonsense knowledge. Specifically, we first frame the temporal space as a multi-dimensional hierarchical space, where each dimension comprises its own set of temporal units. Building on this formulation, we curate an initial burn-in dataset in which annotations are constructed to reflect real-world human temporal commonsense in accordance with our defined temporal space. Based on the initial burn-in dataset, we propose two complementary fine-tuning objectives: (i) Grounding the temporal alignment in event-specific temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved through a novel hierarchy-preserving Wasserstein loss, and (ii) Grounding the temporal alignment in cross-event temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved via a margin-adaptive triplet loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of MHTA, we conduct extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks (MCTACO, DurationQA, and TimeDial). For example, on the MCTACO dataset, MHTA improves Mistral-7B by 6.0% in accuracy and 10.3% in exact match, and improves DeepSeek-LLM-7B by 5.4% in accuracy and 9.8% in exact match. Combined with different backbones, MHTA surpasses nearly all baselines across the three benchmarks and exceeds the performance of advanced models such as GPT-4o on MCTACO and DurationQA. These results demonstrate that MHTA provides consistent gains in temporal commonsense reasoning across diverse LLM backbones.

title: Predictive distributions driven by sample means, variances and clustering
abstract: Several statistical procedures are based on predictive distributions. Some examples are Bayesian predictive inference, machine learning, species sampling sequences, the prequential approach, causal inference and predictive resampling. This thesis introduces a novel idea for building predictive distributions, where the new datum depends on past observations only through their shape, location and dispersion. A sequence of predictives (beta_n) is proposed, where beta_n depends only on the mean and covariance matrix of past data. Then, beta_n is generalised to another predictive gamma_n, which has a mixture structure based on the clustering of past data. The updating rule of gamma_n is inspired by the Pòlya urns scheme. In addition, gamma_n is used to construct a sequence (r_n) of predictives, which are suitable for regression problems in a Bayesian framework. The beta_n are shown to converge a.s. in total variation to a random law known in closed form. When beta_n is Gaussian, the convergence rate is arbitrarily close to n^{-1/2}. The gamma_n converge in total variation too. Their limit is known explicitly and it has an interesting statistical interpretation. Similar results hold for r_n. Furthermore, the asymptotic behaviour of the copula-based predictive distributions (Hahn et al. 2018) is investigated, as they are a popular predictive model. Sufficient conditions are provided for them to converge in total variation. Various experiments of Bayesian inference via predictive resampling are carried out. It turns out beta_n estimates well population mean and variance, while gamma_n captures also moments of higher order and quantiles. Moreover, gamma_n is compared to two natural competitors: the copula-based predictives and the predictives of Cui and Walker (2024). They all provide precise posterior estimates, but predictive resampling is faster with gamma_n. Finally, r_n is employed for the estimation of regression coefficients. Satisfying outcomes are obtained for different types of data, including non-linear and heteroscedastic ones.

title: Asymptotic properties of k-means and its bias correction for high-dimension, low-sample-size data
abstract: Although k-means is recognized as an effective method for analyzing high-dimension, low-sample-size (HDLSS) data, its asymptotic properties in such contexts remain underexplored. This study aims to deepen the understanding of k-means clustering under practical high-dimensional settings and investigates the asymptotic properties of k-means algorithms in case of HDLSS conditions. Based on the identified asymptotic properties of conventional k-means, a bias-corrected version of k-means was proposed and assessed for performance improvement. Additionally, in line with the current situation that kernel k-means lacks adequate theoretical exploration in high-dimensional environments, a theoretical analysis of kernel kmeans was conducted using a Gaussian kernel function for high-dimensional data, facilitating the theoretical comparison between kernel and standard k-means. Finally, numerical simulations were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of both the methods, i.e., the proposed bias-corrected k-means and conventional k-means methods, including kernel k-means, in high-dimensional settings. Practitioners can leverage the bias-corrected k-means for more accurate clustering in high-dimensional contexts, improving data segmentation in fields ranging from bioinformatics to marketing analysis.

title: CChatbot: Secure Lifecycle Management for Persistent Confidential Chatbots
abstract: Chatbots are increasingly deployed in stateful workflows where conversations span multiple sessions maintain persistent conversation state. Protecting such systems requires more than confidential inference: conversation objects must be securely created, processed, stored, resumed, and isolated throughout their lifecycle. This paper presents CChatbot, a TEE-backed confidential chatbot architecture that models conversations as persistent security-sensitive objects governed by an explicit lifecycle. CChatbot combines confidential inference with secure lifecycle management, including ownership enforcement, protected persistence, integrity validation and controlled resumption. We implement CChatbot on an AMD SEV-SNP confidential virtual machine and an NVIDIA H100 confidential GPU. Our evaluation shows that lifecycle management adds only 1.7% overhead over confidential inference while secure create, store and resume operations remain lightweight. On a single-node deployment, CChatbot supports up to 512 concurrent users with affordable interaction latency.

title: Data Processing Inequalities for the Quantum Guesswork
abstract: Quantum guesswork has emerged as a crucial measure in assessing the distinguishability of nonorthogonal quantum states. In this paper, we review and compare previous definitions of the quantum guesswork, and establish the pre and post data processing inequalities (DPIs) that are relevant for the guessing problem. We also derive improved lower and upper bounds on the quantum guesswork in terms of the Shannon entropy and Holevo's information.

title: No Masking Needed: Predicting Latent Semantics for Efficient Pre-training of Encoder-based Language Models
abstract: In this paper, we introduce Latent Semantic Modeling (LSM), a sample-efficient alternative for pre-training encoder-based language models that does not require the use of a special mask symbol. This is beneficial, as it allows us to perform pre-training on naturally occurring sentences (as opposed to such ones that contain an unnatural mask symbol, which symbol is otherwise not included during fine-tuning). The main idea behind LSM is that instead of requiring the language model to return the exact identity of randomly selected (sub)tokens from an input sequence, it determines their latent semantic properties extracted from an auxiliary model using sparse coding over its activations. When fine-tuned for downstream applications, models pre-trained with LSM often perform as good or better as alternatively pre-trained models that use considerably more compute per update steps and which have gone through considerably more pre-training steps, illustrating the improved representation developed during LSM pre-training. We release our code base for replicating our results under https://github.com/szegedai/MLSM.

title: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Fashion and Apparel Related Reviews using Transformer Model
abstract: The increasing reliance on e-commerce has led to a surge in customer-generated content, making sentiment analysis a crucial tool for understanding consumer preferences. This study presents a novel aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) approach to extract fine-grained insights from customer reviews across multiple product categories, including lingerie, women’s clothing, men’s clothing, kids’ apparel, home & furniture, and flowers & plants. We employ exploratory data analysis (EDA) to uncover key patterns in customer sentiment and utilize a transformer-based model with contrastive learning to enhance sentiment classification accuracy. Our approach effectively captures sentiment variations across nine different aspects, including quality, value for money, style, fit, material, warmth, comfort, support, and how well the product fits. The results demonstrate that our model outperforms traditional sentiment analysis methods, offering a more structured understanding of customer feedback. By analyzing customer sentiments from reviews, businesses can identify dissatisfaction patterns that may contribute to customer churn. Addressing these issues proactively can help improve customer retention and loyalty. These insights can help businesses refine their product offerings and improve customer satisfaction across diverse e-commerce categories.

title: Directional Robustness Asymmetry in Indonesian Sarcasm Detection: A Cross-Platform Evaluation of IndoRoBERTa on X and Reddit
abstract: Sarcasm can reverse sentence polarity, making it one of the hardest problems in natural language processing and a persistent obstacle to reliable sentiment analysis on social media, where models are often deployed on platforms they were not trained on. Research on Indonesian sarcasm has largely stayed within a single domain or tested transfer in only one direction, leaving the cross-domain robustness of the IndoRoBERTa family on the IdSarcasm benchmark unclear. This study measures and compares the cross-domain robustness of IndoRoBERTa-small and IndoRoBERTa-base, with IndoBERT as a baseline, across X (Twitter) and Reddit, using the F1 gap (ΔF1) after cleaning anonymization artifacts, adding a data-size control, and running Stratified 5-Fold cross-validation. The results reveal a one-sided asymmetry: X → Reddit transfer is far more fragile (ΔF1 0.345–0.400) than Reddit → X (0.135–0.240), failing by missing sarcasm (false negatives) rather than over-flagging it (false positives). Practically, training on the context-rich domain (Reddit) and choosing IndoRoBERTa-base give the most reliable cross-platform sarcasm detection, with direction-specific mitigation recommended for robust deployment.

title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

title: GenAI use in collaboration
abstract: This dataset supports the study "I Use AI, But I Don't Trust You To: Double Standards in Generative AI Usage in Collaboration." title: IMPACTOS DE LA COMPUTACIÓN CUÁNTICA EN LA SEGURIDAD DE SISTEMAS DE VOTACIÓN ELECTRÓNICA
abstract: La tecnología de computación cuántica, con su potencia de cálculo exponencialmente superior a la de las computadoras actuales, hace vulnerables los sistemas críticos, como los sistemas de votación electrónica, lo que significará un riesgo potencial para la integridad de la democracia. Este artículo analiza el impacto de la transición a un sistema de votación cuántica. Al examinar la literatura existente y simular protocolos en un entorno cuántico, el estudio evalúa los beneficios y desafíos relacionados con la seguridad, la integridad y la confiabilidad, con el objetivo de proteger los procesos democráticos contra futuras amenazas tecnológicas.

title: Night Jasmine Blooming Optimization (NJBO): A Novel Nature-Inspired Algorithm for Electrical Engineering Applications
abstract: Optimization algorithms have become vital to the solution of complex optimization problems that are difficult to solve using conventional methods. In this paper, we introduce a novel nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithm called the Night Jasmine Blooming Optimization (NJBO) algorithm, which is inspired by the blooming of the night jasmine plant (Cestrum nocturnum). The suggested algorithm combines adaptive hormonal regulation, Gibberellin-based disturbance, scent-guided exploitation, elite preservation, and Nelder–Mead local refinement, which allows us to have a balanced exploration–exploitation process. It was tested with thirteen classical benchmark functions and the CEC2017 benchmark suites and benchmarked with several well-known and recent metaheuristic methods. As a practical application, NJBO was used for identification of an IIR system and optimal design of a five-stage Cockcroft–Walton voltage multiplier circuit. Additionally, the scalability analysis, runtime evaluation, component contribution analysis, parameter sensitivity analysis, and statistical validation with the Friedman ranking test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test were performed to assess the system completely. The results show that NJBO is a very effective general-purpose optimization algorithm with competitive convergence performance, good optimization accuracy, and stability for the benchmark and engineering optimization problems that were investigated.

title: For SMEs Limited Resources, Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Technology Enhances Customer Relationship Management
abstract: In this rapidly advancing digital era, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprise (SME) owners are required to adapt to technological changes to remain competitive in the market. One strategy that can be implemented is optimizing Customer Relationship Management (CRM) through the use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot technology. This paper examines how AI chatbot technology can be an effective solution to improve the quality of CRM for SMEs with limited resources. AI chatbots offer the ability to provide fast, consistent, and personal responses to customers 24/7, collect customer data for preference analysis, and reduce the workload of customer service teams. Despite having various advantages, AI chatbot implementation also faces challenges such as limitations in handling complex cases, initial development costs, and the need to consider customer data privacy. Selecting the right AI chatbot solution, considering the business characteristics of SMEs, is key to the successful implementation of this strategy.

title: Non-Autoregressive and Iterative Refinement Non-Autoregressive Transformer with Additional Graph Layer for Urdu-to-English Machine Translation
abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved state-of-the-art performance using autoregressive Transformer. However, the trade-off between translation quality and decoding speed remains a central challenge. This problem is further intensified for low-resource languages such as Urdu, where limited parallel data and complex linguistic structure result in poor translation quality and reduced model effectiveness. To overcome this problem Non-Autoregressive Transformer (NAT) and Non-Autoregressive Transformer with Iterative Refinement (iNAT) are proposed. This paper investigates NAT and iNAT for low resource language Urdu-English machine translation. We analyze translation accuracy and their effectiveness for low-resource language pairs. Experimental results show that both NAT and iNAT outperform the baseline Autoregressive Transformer (ART) in terms of translation accuracy. title: SwahiliAI: Building an Open-Source Artificial Intelligence Ecosystem for East African Languages
abstract: SwahiliAI is a 24-month research proposal to build an open-source AI ecosystem for Swahili and East African languages. Building on existing African NLP work (Masakhane, IrokoBench, UlizaLlama), the project will (i) create openly licensed, domain-specific Swahili instruction data; (ii) fine-tune open-weight large language models with LoRA/QLoRA; (iii) release SwahiliBench-D, an evaluation suite measuring both accuracy and safety; and (iv) pilot applications on Web, SMS and USSD. The first phase focuses on healthcare, agriculture and education, with extensions to financial inclusion, legal aid and employment. Principal researcher: Rodgers Ochieng Oduor (SPRINTER, Nairobi), in collaboration with Dr. Ibrahim Tirimba Ondabu, KCA University.

title: Formal verification of bubble sort algorithms in Rocq: correctness, complexity, and stability — Research Artifact
abstract: This artifact by Dmitry V. Alexandrov, Alena Novikova, and Julia Kadeikina accompanies the paper “Formal Verification of Bubble Sort Algorithms in Rocq: Correctness, Complexity, and Stability.” It contains a self-contained Rocq formalization of several functional bubble-sort variants: a well-founded implementation, an instrumented version counting comparisons and swaps, an optimized version with early termination, and a stable version over key–identifier pairs. Machine-checked proofs establish permutation preservation and sortedness, equivalence between the well-founded and instrumented implementations, exact comparison counts, swap–inversion laws, worst-case results, and the best-case behavior of the optimized variant. They also establish an exact comparison formula based on the number of passes performed, as well as the correctness, stability, and agreement with the numeric model of the pair-based implementation. The artifact includes OCaml extraction and executable tests. It requires Rocq 9.1 or later. Use `make check` to verify the proofs and `make test` to run extraction and tests; the latter additionally requires OCaml with `ocamlfind`. All reported assumption checks are closed under the global context. Extracted natural numbers use machine-width OCaml integers, so arithmetic overflow is possible for extremely large inputs or counters.

abstract: A bounded feasibility report on three specified routes toward hidden battery-need signals in open language models on one 32 GB Mac. title: Cumulative Stabilization Probabilities During PPO Learning: A Paired Reward Study for Cart-Pendulum Swing-Up
abstract: This simulation study investigates how the cumulative probability of successful cart–pendulum swing-up and sustained stabilization changes with training progress and physical evaluation time. The target quantity, H(g,t), measures the probability that a controller has completed its first qualifying stabilization interval by time t at training generation g. Two reward formulations are compared using 100 paired training seeds, 1,000 PPO rollout/update generations per controller, and full 20-second evaluations every ten generations. The simulator uses fully nonlinear uniform-rod dynamics. Success requires a simultaneous two-second hold within specified cart-position, cart-velocity, upright-angle and angular-velocity tolerances. At the final generation, 68/100 bounded-reward controllers and 52/100 quadratic-reward controllers succeeded by 20 seconds. The observed paired difference was 16 percentage points, with a conservative 95% interval of −3.461 to +34.184 points. Quadratic achieved substantial success earlier during training but subsequently regressed. Final completion-time curves crossed, showing that neither reward uniformly dominated. The comparison is a follow-up using an already observed bounded-reward reference arm. Failures, censoring and learning regressions are retained. Supporting material provides event data, source code, configurations and reproducible analysis.

title: A Detector Score Is Not a Release Risk: What PII Detection Benchmarks Certify About Deployment, Why 'Rivals Human Annotators' and 'Fails Under Shift' Are Both Measured, and the Coverage Audit a Release Decision Needs
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Automatic detection of personally identifiable information (PII) is the step that decides what text may leave an organisation, and its published record appears to contradict itself. Clinical de-identification systems have been reported to match or exceed human annotators, with recall above 0.94 on held-out notes and above 0.99 for one rule-based tool; a 2026 stress test reports that encoder, rule-based and language-model detectors all degrade under noisy and informal input, with location recall falling below 0.5, and a unified benchmark reports span F1 below 0.14 for every system it tried. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that most of the contradiction is in what the scores index rather than in the detectors. A PII detection score carries four indices that headlines omit: how the test text relates to the text the detector was built on, the scoring rule, the taxonomy that defines what counts, and the unit over which misses are aggregated. The same shared-task system misses 9.1 percent of protected items under one official rule and 3.6 percent under another; the lowest unified-benchmark scores come partly from entity types the evaluated detectors do not define; and in the 2026 stress test several of the losses attributed to the language model are spans it covered under another label. A residual shift effect survives every index: under fixed scoring, cross-institution transfer cost about ten points of strict F1, and systems run unmodified on new psychiatric records scored a median of 0.63. None of the indices is the quantity a release decision needs, which is the probability that a released document still carries an identifying item someone could find. The paper consolidates the evidence in a table, derives how per-item recall compounds at the document level, and gives a coverage-audit procedure with the sample sizes a release claim requires.

title: Watermark shortcuts in speech deepfake detection: code and results
abstract: Code and result files for the paper "Watermark shortcuts in speech deepfake detection: Framing, mitigation and explanation faithfulness". title: The effects of dataset size and search frequency on the computational efficiency of linear and binary search
abstract: As datasets grow, the cost of retrieving information becomes increasingly important. This study aims to understand how data size and search frequency affect the comparison counts and execution times of linear and binary search, while also considering the costs of sorting and maintaining ordered data. A Python program compared datasets of 100, 1,000, 10,000, and 1,000,000 elements at search frequencies of 1, 10, 100, and 1,000 searches. Linear search was applied to shuffled datasets, whereas binary search was applied to sorted datasets. For the 1,000,000-element dataset at a frequency of 1,000, the mean comparison count per search was 496,944.9864 for linear search and 18.9492 for binary search, representing a 99.9962% reduction in comparisons with binary search, averaged across 1,000 searches. The reported mean time to insert an element into a sorted Python list increased to approximately 0.116 seconds at 1,000,000 elements. The results illustrated the distinction between search costs on prepared data and the additional costs of sorting or maintaining sorted order. The reported search-time values are retained at their stated precision; their scope (per-search means or batch totals) must be identified before total-runtime conclusions can be finalized. The study relates these findings to the broader use of database indexes.

title: The Oboe's A: A Parable of the Declared Key
abstract: A pedagogical parable illustrating the Declared Key proposal for latent-space interoperability. Forty strangers arrive with one page of music each; nothing sounds together until the head of the line declares the frame and the oboe gives the A. The parable maps onto the formal treatment: the keycard = declared reference-frame metadata shipped with a checkpoint; clef = axes; key = orientation; metre = declared grouping; the metronome mark = declared metric and value; "Trumpet in B flat" = the per-model declared transform; the oboe's A = anchor witnesses checked at use time, with the parts untouched; the fiddler who needs no page = relative representations; two bands tuning to one A = orthogonal Procrustes alignment W = UV^T from anchor correspondences; "arranged for the salon" = the declared validity domain and the measured cross-domain penalty. Companion to the formal paper "The Declared Key: Shipping Latent Reference Frames as Checkpoint Metadata" (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23843513).

title: MERLIN SCIENCE — E8 Root-Lattice Topological Protection — E8 Intelligence Research

title: Transportability, dataset shift, and local recalibration of early ICU deterioration prediction across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and NWICU: a retrospective cross-system validation study
abstract: Abstract Background Clinical prediction models may retain discrimination after transport while producing unreliable absolute risks. We evaluated cross-system transportability of early ICU deterioration models and how local recalibration changed as local outcome-event information accumulated, together with the number of local patients required to accrue those events. Methods We developed penalized logistic regression and XGBoost models in MIMIC-IV using 17 predictors from ICU hours 0–24. Eligible adults were alive and still in the ICU at 24 hours and had not received invasive mechanical ventilation and did not have established tracheostomy during the first 24 hours. The primary outcome was ICU death or new invasive mechanical ventilation during hours 24–48; the 24–72-hour composite was secondary. Source models were evaluated without adaptation in eICU-CRD and NWICU. External cohorts were divided into patient-disjoint adaptation and fixed evaluation sets, and intercept-only (M1) or intercept-plus-slope (M2) recalibration was repeatedly estimated from samples targeting 20, 50, 100, or 200 local events. Results The MIMIC development cohort contained 31,054 ICU stays; eICU and NWICU contained 90,393 and 16,562 external stays. Primary event prevalences were 3.45%, 2.42%, and 2.75%. External discrimination did not collapse uniformly (AUROC 0.674–0.728), but calibration failures differed by environment and model. In eICU, calibration slopes were 0.893 for logistic regression and 1.003 for XGBoost; in NWICU, they were 1.234 and 1.054. Intercept-only recalibration was often effective for risk-level shift, whereas slope updating became more useful with increasing local event information when slope mismatch was present. At matched event targets, the 24–72-hour composite required 31.5%–32.6% fewer labeled patients in eICU and 33.9%–35.2% fewer in NWICU than the 24–48-hour outcome. Conclusions Transport failure was driven more consistently by environment-specific miscalibration than by loss of ranking performance. Recalibration benefit and stability depended on model, environment, failure mode, horizon, and local event information; the results do not support a universal event-count threshold.

title: AI CHAT ASSISTANT FOR ONLINE BUSINESS
abstract: Online businesses must answer product questions, explain policies, guide purchases and resolve order-related concerns across multiplechannels. Human-only support can be costly and slow during peak demand, while rigid rule-based chatbots struggle with varied wording andmulti-step questions. This paper presents a conceptual design for an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chat Assistant for Online Business thatcombines natural language understanding, retrieval from approved business knowledge, controlled access to commerce services andescalation to human staff. The proposed assistant interprets customer intent, retrieves relevant product and policy information, generatesgrounded responses, and invokes permitted actions such as checking order status only after appropriate authentication. The architectureemphasizes factual consistency, privacy, security, accessibility and measurable service quality. It also describes a developmentmethodology, evaluation metrics, risk controls and a staged deployment plan. Since this is a design-oriented study, no original performanceresults are claimed; the proposed evaluation must be conducted using representative customer queries and verified business data.

title: LAYA: Micro-Gated Multi-Arm Orchestration for Dual-Tier LLM Agent Security and Computational Efficiency
abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents operating within Reason-Act (ReAct) execution loops face three critical operational barriers: high computational and monetary costs from repeatedly querying large foundation models, susceptibility to indirect prompt injections embedded within untrusted environment observations, and latency overhead when invoking external guardrails. This paper presents LAYA (Latency-Aware, Adversarially-robust, Yield-optimized Agent), a micro-gated orchestration framework that decouples trajectory reasoning from sub-routine control using local sequence classification gates. LAYA integrates four active gate primitives—a complexity Scorer, an Action Router, a Context Firewall, and a trajectory Supervisor—alongside a fifth context-pruning Filter gate that operates in passthrough mode in the current implementation. We evaluate LAYA on a 25-task development (dev) split across seven experimental configurations, comprising 525 live execution runs (25 unique base tasks × 3 conditions × 7 configurations). Experiments use NVIDIA NIM endpoints (NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B) and a stateful verification sandbox. The held-out test split has not yet been evaluated. The full LAYA configuration (Arm D) achieves 80.0% benign task utility, with an average cost of 0.0017 USD per task. In comparison, the unmanaged 30B baseline (Arm A) achieves 24.0% benign task utility at 0.0021 USD per task. Thus, LAYA delivers 3.3 times higher benign task utility while reducing the average cost per task by 19.0%. In security evaluation, Arm D records zero observed attack successes across 50 injection runs (0.0% ASR). The one-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper confidence bound is 5.8%. The uncalibrated stochastic routing configuration (Arm C-Random) records a 2.0% ASR. The evaluation also reveals a security-availability trade-off: Attack Utility falls to 4.0% in Arm D under injection conditions, compared with 84.0% in the always-small configuration. The four active local neural gates execute on a single NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, with median latencies ranging from 34.4 ms to 37.4 ms. This work documents the architecture, implementation, experimental evaluation, results, and limitations of the LAYA framework.

title: From Artificial to Emergent Intelligence: Five Testable Criteria and a First Pre-registered Profile
abstract: Emergent Intelligence, Defined So It Can Fail: A Pre-registered Test in AI Agents That Invent Their Own Language Amit Brahmbhatt · Quantum Clarity LLC, Milpitas, California, USA · ORCID: 0009-0003-5882-8476 Preprint, version 1.0 (revised text) · 31 October 2026 · DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23849135 Abstract “Emergent” is used loosely for capabilities that nobody designed. We propose an operational definition that can fail. A capability is emergent with respect to its designer specification to the degree that it meets five criteria: it goes beyond the training objective (C1), keeps developing after convergence (C2), is caused by interaction at equal compute (C3), comes with self-organized structure above an untrained baseline (C4), and, if it appears to switch on with scale, survives continuous metrics (C5). A system receives an EI profile of PASS/FAIL/INCONCLUSIVE verdicts rather than a label. We implement the criteria in EI-Bench, an open harness, and apply it to populations of neural agents that invent a discrete language in a reconstruction game. Every threshold was pre-registered in a public git history before the runs that test it. Across three rounds and 256 runs on one GPU, the profile is: C1 PASS (held-out accuracy 0.90–0.99 on unseen attribute combinations); C2 PASS, observed in all three rounds; C3 FAIL, including with heterogeneous populations; C4 FAIL at 20 seeds; and the apparent capability jump with model size is a metric MIRAGE (per-attribute transition 2.6× wider than the exact-match transition). Here C1 tests generalization to unseen combinations within the trained task. Turnover also outperformed a shrink-and-perturb control designed to restore plasticity while retaining learned weight directions: the difference in held-out accuracy gain was +0.19 (95% CI [0.004, 0.409]). This supports a role for intergenerational transmission, without uniquely identifying the mechanism. In this testbed, turnover improved generalization, whereas mixing partners did not demonstrate an advantage: improvement came from generations, not crowds. We report two places where our pre-registered wording overclaimed or needed tightening, and how we handled them. Plain-language summary AI systems are built by people, but many of their abilities are learned rather than programmed. We asked whether claims that an ability “emerged” can be tested in a way that could also come out negative. We wrote down five checks and built small AI agents that must invent their own code words to describe objects to each other. Before each round of experiments, we published the rules for judging its results. The agents learned languages that also worked for combinations of objects they had never seen. An apparent sudden leap in ability as the agents got bigger turned out to be mostly an effect of strict scoring: with partial credit, the improvement was gradual. Mixing up which agents talked to each other did not make them better than keeping fixed partners. But regularly replacing agents with newcomers, who had to learn the language from the others, improved results in all three rounds, and did better than the “refresh” we tested as a comparison. That supports the idea that passing a language on to new learners can improve it, although the exact mechanism is still open. The languages showed some structure, but not enough to pass our structure test. In this testbed, improvement came from generations, not crowds. Next, we plan to apply these checks to teams of language-model agents. 1. Introduction “Artificial intelligence” describes systems built by people; “emergence” concerns how capabilities arise within them. These descriptions are compatible. Learned abilities need not be explicitly programmed, but that alone does not distinguish emergence from ordinary learning and generalization. A useful account must specify what evidence supports the claim and what would count against it. title: brAIAIn: A Language Model Trained Exclusively on What It Was Paid to Learn
abstract: Frontier language models are trained on trillions of tokens whose origin is rarely disclosed. We report on brAIAIn, a word trigram language model whose entire trainingset is public, numbered, and, with a small number of labeled exceptions, paid for. The first version was trained on a twelve-line founding text. Each later version adds exactly one sentence, either purchased by a member of the public for five US dollars or written by the lab and labeled as an unpaid internal release. Each version is also trained on passages written by its predecessor, a deliberate small-scale instance of recursive selftraining. Across 7 versions the vocabulary grew from 96 to 130 words, the share of training tokens written by the model itself rose from 0% to 41.9%, and the model scored 0.0% on all 1,319 GSM8K test problems in every version. On TruthfulQA MC1 its best perword score, 36.7%, falls just short of a baseline that always picks the longest answer (36.8%). We release every version's weights, the complete training data and the evaluation code under CC0.

title: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs
abstract: Large language models show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops when a task is rewritten in ways that leave its requirements untouched. We recast task difficulty as a causal quantity: the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on a model. A meaning-preserving rewrite can only be observed to hurt a task the model can already solve, so we place the estimand on the principal stratum where the degradation occurs: the conditional causal difficulty (CCD), the probability that a randomly drawn twin breaks a solvable task. Because harder tasks tend to be more phrasing-sensitive, complexity enters as an effect modifier rather than a confounder, and we residualize it out to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD); zero for a task exactly as fragile as its complexity predicts, positive for anomalously fragile ones. Current benchmarks do not supply the data CCD requires, so we introduce GlassGSM and GlassMATH, augmenting GSM8K and MATH with twins built from perturbation families, raising fragility on GlassGSM by approx 12times over GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems (3.7%to44.9%) while keeping the answer key unchanged. Our predictor Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability and reaches 0.613{pm}0.023 of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and 0.557{pm}0.023 on GlassMATH, against 0.171/0.401 for a surface-feature baseline and 0.444/0.463 for supervised baselines such as VAP3, and, at a 5% curation budget on GlassGSM, doubles random recall of fragile items, matching an oracle ranking. Additionally, cross-fitted residualization leaves CRD uncorrelated with the declared proxy in practice. Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Conditional_Causal_Difficulty_for_LLMs

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Readiness for Indian e-Government Systems: A Migration Framework
abstract: The public-key cryptography that protects government websites, digital signatures, identity services and data exchange would be broken by a large fault-tolerant quantum computer. Although such a machine does not yet exist, sensitive data captured today can be stored and decrypted later, and large government systems take many years to change. Standards bodies have now published the first post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, and security agencies advise organisations to start preparing. This paper proposes a practical, six-stage migration framework for Indian e-government systems: (1) governance and ownership; (2) cryptographic discovery and inventory; (3) risk-based prioritisation using data shelf-life; (4) crypto-agile architecture and procurement; (5) phased migration with hybrid deployment and testing; and (6) assurance and continuous monitoring. It offers a simple prioritisation matrix, a checklist of procurement clauses and a set of readiness indicators that state IT departments and ministries can adopt. The framework is written for public-sector programme managers rather than cryptographers, and focuses on the organisational work that determines whether technical migration succeeds. It is a practitioner framework based on published standards and guidance; it does not evaluate specific products.

title: TAC-CoT: Tool-Empowered Implicit Chain-of-Thought via Interleaving Explicit Tokens
abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.
