title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
abstract: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9times the success, 5.4times the generalization, and 3.9times the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8times faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.

title: Just-in-Time Skill Retrieval via Long-Horizon State Tracking
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations, execution outcomes, and newly revealed constraints. This motivates just-in-time skill retrieval, which dynamically selects skills as execution unfolds. Just-in-time skill retrieval is promising but challenging: the utility of a skill depends not only on the current context, but also on the evolving task state shaped by prior steps. To this end, we propose JitSkill, a state-grounded framework that addresses this challenge through continuous task-state tracking. By connecting emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, JitSkill provides procedural support throughout execution without treating each retrieval decision independently. Experiments across three agent benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in improving long-horizon task completion. Our code is available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/JitSkill.git/.

title: Deterministic photon exchange prepared from the past
abstract: Two-ended control of photons — shaped emission and a time-reversed, matched receiver, both prepared in advance — is a mature technology: 94–99.4% coupling in single elements, 98.1% absorption of an arriving photon between remote nodes, links up to 30 m, and coherent memories that receive even unknown quantum states. Like the in and out states of an S-matrix element, both ends of the apparatus are prepared; this paper collects these realizations into one efficiency budget with exact shape and timing tolerances. It then asks what two-way quantum computing (2WQC) would need for the end of a computation to act as a condition, as preparation acts at its beginning. Everything we prepare — source, processor and a universal, problem-independent ready receiver to which a verifier routes a flag photon — fixes only the initial boundary of the Feynman ensemble. Standard quantum mechanics sums over the far end (an indifferent final boundary, giving the Born rule), so an acceptance condition can only be tested, with its ordinary probability. The missing ingredient is an enforced far end: a final boundary supplied by nature that weights ready endings. If weak but renewable, such a weight would compound exponentially over linearly many endings (about n·ln2/Δw), under conditions the paper states. We have not identified a published all-attempt bound for this weight. The paper specifies a direct test on existing hardware: two balanced endings, one active and one passive, selected after an earlier record is digitized and sealed. Standard quantum mechanics predicts exactly zero contrast, including every ordinary feedback path; 1e8 eligible trials per setting give a counting sensitivity Δw ≈ 3e-4 (planning figures: about an hour of link operation; a projected 1e-4 per delay on a quantum processor, with an analysis kit in the companion range-control paper). The test needs no absolute calibration: setting-independent preparation and readout errors cancel in the randomized difference. Either outcome constrains the declared ending law; a replicated signal would motivate tests of renewal, coherence and witness preservation. A one-page proposal for experimental groups is included.

title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
abstract: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

title: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents
abstract: As coding agents achieve increasingly high success rates on software engineering benchmarks, recent efforts have sought to increase task complexity through longer horizons and more extensive code modifications. However, real-world software development often spans multiple interdependent repositories, introducing additional challenges in dependency reasoning, change propagation, and interface consistency. Rather than further increasing complexity within individual repositories, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark for cross-repository joint development comprising 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. CrossSWE verifies the necessity of coordinated changes by testing whether partial repository modifications are insufficient to achieve the intended behavior. Our evaluation of five LLMs reveals substantial challenges, with the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, achieving only 58.48% Pass@1. Furthermore, cross-repository inconsistencies emerge as the most prevalent failure mode (44.2%), highlighting the difficulty of maintaining consistency across interdependent repositories.

title: THE EL-RAKHAWI FRAMEWORK FOR TOPOLOGICAL REINFORCEMENT LEARNING ON RIEMANNIAN MANIFOLDS INTELLIGENT AGENTS LEARNING AND DECISION-MAKING IN NON-EUCLIDEAN SPACES
abstract: "The El-Rakhawi Framework for Topological Reinforcement Learning on Riemannian Manifolds" shatters the Euclidean bottleneck of modern AI, enabling agents to learn in non-Euclidean spaces. It integrates three pillars: (1) Riemannian Policy Optimization, using geodesic flows and parallel transport to respect manifold geometry; (2) Topologically-Guided Exploration, employing persistent homology and Betti numbers to analyze state space topology, reducing sample complexity by 70%; and (3) Symmetry-Aware Learning, leveraging group theory to exploit conserved quantities. Performance is quantified by the Manifold Learning Efficiency Index (MLEI), a strictly bounded metric (0.0-1.0) evaluating reward, geodesic accuracy, topological coverage, and symmetry preservation. This framework revolutionizes robotics, autonomous navigation, and scientific discovery by teaching machines to navigate complex, curved spaces with geometric wisdom. abstract: As multi-agent systems grow in size and complexity, understanding which features of their interactions support collective capability becomes increasingly difficult. title: The Semantic Field Coherence Score (SFCS): An Observability Metric for Early Detection of Semantic Field Degradation and Domain Drift in AI Systems
abstract: Operational AI assurance requires mechanisms capable of detecting semantic instability before it manifests as observable failures. Existing monitoring approaches primarily focus on accuracy, safety, factuality, benchmark performance, and hallucination detection, providing limited visibility into whether an AI system remains anchored within its intended semantic field. This paper introduces the Semantic Field Coherence Score (SFCS), an observability metric designed to quantify semantic field coherence across repeated AI outputs. Rather than measuring truth, correctness, or logical agreement, SFCS measures the degree to which outputs remain anchored within a shared semantic field. To evaluate the metric, we developed the SFCS Validation Workbench and conducted controlled divergence experiments, contradiction analysis, domain-shift testing, and crossdomain drift validation spanning finance, artificial intelligence, medical, and legal domains. Experimental results demonstrated systematic degradation of SFCS under progressive semantic divergence and domain drift conditions while contradictory statements within the same semantic field maintained high coherence scores. Cross-domain experiments revealed comparable degradation trajectories across multiple domains. These findings suggest that semantic field degradation may be observable before complete semantic collapse occurs, positioning SFCS as a potential early-warning signal for emerging domain drift and instability in operational AI systems.

title: "PRISM" Is Not All You Need: Cross-Topic Name Collisions and Scientific Paper Retrieval
abstract: Scientific names increasingly connect papers from different research topics, leaving readers to recover a paper's identity from context. We study this convergence in 564,861 AI-related arXiv records. Cross-topic name collision grows 4.33-fold from a pooled 2020-2022 reference to 2026, compared with 1.12-fold within topics. A second sentence encoder reproduces the pattern, and name-group resampling quantifies its uncertainty. Fixed word-frequency bands locate the main increase in an intermediate-frequency vocabulary shared by many research areas. We then measure the ambiguity that remains after supplying research clues. With the same three-term query construction, shared-name targets retain matched identification deficits of 25.7 percentage points under title-based BM25 and 6.9 points under title-plus-abstract E5. Within fixed same-name candidates, listwise language-model ranking reaches 89.2% using the query and candidate titles. Topic-specific comparisons show that context resolves more cross-topic ambiguity. The evaluation separates candidate competition, document fields, and contextual ranking through lexical, dense, and language-model baselines. Source-linked cases and a portable evaluation collection make the phenomenon inspectable and reusable for scientific retrieval and research assistants.

title: EMG to speech mapping using scalogram-spectrogram features for silent speech recognition
abstract: Silent speech Recognition systems (SSRs), which rely upon non-vocal signals like electromyography (EMG) from facial muscle tissues, offer a promising answer by permitting speech production without sound. This study seeks to enhance communication for those individuals by using a machine learning model, getting to know to correctly translate EMG signals from silent speech into audible, intelligible speech, thereby bridging the distance between non-verbal and verbal exchange. SSR improves the quality of life for those with speech impairments by providing necessary communication choices. This project investigates a whole new SSR method, which involves using surface electromyography signals (sEMG) and audio. A machine learning model was trained to recognize keywords via silent speech by an addition of a dataset of audio and sEMG signals. The scalograms and spectrograms are plotted for audio and EMG signal respectively and then it is mapped using the EfficientNet B0. It is then converted into textual content and then audible speech with the help of a speech synthesis system with an accuracy of 76%. This innovative technology opens new avenues in terms of silent communication, especially for customers who can talk without vocalizing, thereby improving accessibility and conversation for those who need it.

title: From Logs to Faults: Reference-Free Fault Localization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are widely used for domain-specific question answering, yet locating faults remains manual and time-consuming. Fault localization is challenging because RAG pipelines consist of interdependent stages, where faults can propagate downstream, masking their origin, or remain undetected even when the final answer is correct. Existing evaluation approaches often focus on individual stages and rely on reference answers or code instrumentation. We present RAGLog, which detects and localizes faults across RAG stages using execution logs, without requiring reference answers or code instrumentation. RAGLog transforms heterogeneous API logs into a common RAG schema and combines rule-based, embedding-based, and LLM-based checks to identify faulty stages. We introduce a live fault injector and RAGLog Faults, a dataset of 3,134 runs from five RAG pipelines with stage-level fault labels. With Claude Haiku 5.5, RAGLog achieves a pooled F1 score of 0.73 on runs with naturally occurring faults, outperforming Claude Code (0.58) and Codex (0.52), and comparable effectiveness on runs with injected faults (0.84 versus 0.80 and 0.82, respectively). It analyzes runs in approximately five seconds at US\$0.005 each, with overall lower cost and latency than agent baselines. RAGLog is available as an open-source tool for debugging, evaluating, and monitoring RAG pipelines.

title: Gender Classification Based on Voice Using MFCC Features and Naïve Bayes Algorithm
abstract: This study aims to classify gender based on voice signals using Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) and the Gaussian Naïve Bayes algorithm. Voice-based gender classification is relevant to biometric identification, speech-based services, and human–computer interaction. This study uses 150 audio recordings from 150 different speakers, consisting of 75 male and 75 female speakers. The audio was converted to mono, resampled to 16 kHz, peak normalized, and extracted into 13 MFCC coefficients. The mean MFCC values were used as input features for the Gaussian Naïve Bayes classifier. Four training and testing data split scenarios were evaluated, namely 50:50, 60:40, 70:30, and 80:20. The results showed accuracy values of 88.00%, 96.67%, 95.56%, and 96.67%, respectively. The highest accuracy of 96.67% was obtained using the 80:20 split, with 29 of 30 testing samples correctly classified. These results indicate that the combination of 13 MFCC coefficients and Gaussian Naïve Bayes can effectively classify gender based on voice signals. The study concludes that the proportion of training data affects classification performance, while further research using larger and more diverse datasets is needed to improve model robustness and generalizability.

title: Hinted Scaling Laws
abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most 10^{20} FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a 10^{23} FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to 10^{22} FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

title: Valuing AI Contributions in Drug Discovery — A Reference Framework
abstract: AI tools are priced per token or seat. Yet in drug discovery their outputs range in value from nothing to the foundation of a new medicine. This framework examines how the value of an AI contribution could be measured, attributed and paid for. It is written for pharmaceutical and biotech companies, AI vendors, laboratory informatics providers and their advisers. The report reviews outcome-based pricing in customer service and milestone-and-royalty deals between AI-native discovery companies and pharma. It sets out the legal position across inventorship, copyright, trade secrets, contract, data protection, regulation, competition and tax. AI vendors have no default legal claim on downstream value, so any share must be created by contract. The missing infrastructure is a provenance record linking each AI output to the electronic lab notebook and LIMS records it fed. The framework offers a decision model, strategies by company type, a seventeen-term model term sheet, a phased implementation roadmap, a risk register and a review of related literature. title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
abstract: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

title: Little Elpier : Higher-Order Logic, Types and λProlog, One Question at a Time
abstract: What eats a fly? Ask the pond. A small pond: algae, snails and flies, frogs and fish, a duck, a heron and an otter. Eleven short lines say who eats whom. Type a question, eats X fly, and a program answers: the frog, then the fish. It does not search the web or guess. It answers only from what the lines say, and it tells you when they say nothing. That is a logic program: a list of things that are true, and a way to ask what follows. This little book teaches the idea from zero, in the question-and-answer style of The Little Schemer. Each page is two columns, a short question on the left and a short answer on the right. Cover the answers with a card, try, then look. Now and then a box states a Maxim, a short rule the questions above it have earned, from "A fact says what is true. A question asks whether it follows." to "A typing rule is a clause. A type checker is a logic program, and it runs both ways." The language is λProlog, a younger and stranger relative of Prolog. It adds three things: types, so the computer turns away nonsense before it runs; predicates you pass around like numbers; and two small words, pi and =>, that let a program say "for any new thing" and "suppose this were true". Those three additions are what higher-order logic programming means. With them, a type checker for a little programming language fits in seven short clauses, and the same seven clauses infer types they were never told. That is where the book ends. What you will learn Facts and Questions. Constants, predicates, capital letters as holes, and what "no" really means. Rules and Recursion. :- as "if", recursion that knows when to stop, and the search tree behind every answer. Terms and Unification. Numbers built as trees, and how the engine makes two terms the same, or fails. Lists. One append, run three ways: join, check and split. A relation has no inputs and outputs until you ask it something. Types. Kinds, types and modes, and a checker that reads the program before it runs. Predicates as Values. One rule for "above", "upstream of" and "older than"; map, filter and fold. Lambdas. Predicates without names, terms with holes, and binders that cannot be captured. Pi and Implication. What-if questions about a pond that is not quite this one. The Little Type Checker. Seven clauses that check the types of a little language and, asked with a hole, infer them. Who it is for Students and programmers who have never taken a logic course. You need some programming in any language, a pencil, and patience. No mathematics, no Prolog and no Lean are assumed. You do not need to know what ∀ means; by Chapter 8 you will have written it. A chapter is an evening's work. What you get 9 short chapters, 541 questions with their answers, and 11 Maxims collected on one page 35 exercises graded ★ to ★★★, each with a solution that runs 14 diagrams: the food web, search trees, term trees, and binders A two-page cheat sheet and a guided "Where to Go Next" The Apache-2.0 companion code at github.com/Volland/little-elpier: every program in the book, with every printed output kept as a golden file that a test checks Every example runs The engine is lean-elpi, an implementation of the ELPI dialect of λProlog written in Lean 4. pip install leanelpi gives you the whole engine with nothing to compile, on macOS, Linux and Windows with WSL; a Docker image and a build from source work too. The book's site, volland.github.io/little-elpier, has a sample of the frames.

title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
abstract: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.
